nameStory: The word 'sheep' comes from the Old English 'scēap,' which has been used for these woolly creatures for over a thousand years. The name is perfectly straightforward—no fancy Latin translation or descriptive flourishes needed—because sheep have been such familiar companions to humans throughout history. Sometimes the simplest names stick because they're for the animals we know best!
description: Sheep are medium-sized, stocky mammals with thick, curly wool covering most of their bodies. Adults typically weigh between 100-300 pounds and stand about 2-3 feet tall at the shoulder. They have rectangular pupils, small triangular ears, and faces that can range from white to black to brown. Most sheep you'll see in New England are white or cream-colored, though some breeds come in darker shades.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Dense, curly wool that feels springy and oily to the touch, often with a distinctive lanolin smell—a waxy, slightly sweet scent that protects the fleece from moisture

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Stocky, barrel-shaped body with relatively short legs and a distinctly rectangular build when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Move in tight flocks, following each other in single file along paths, and make characteristic 'baa' bleating sounds, especially when separated from the group

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Split-hoof tracks about 2-3 inches long, showing two distinct toe marks that form a heart-like shape in soft mud or snow

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Small, dark, pellet-like droppings scattered in clusters, and paths worn smooth from repeated use by the flock

habitat: In New England, sheep are found on farms and pastures, particularly in hilly areas with good drainage and open grassland. They prefer rolling meadows and fields with access to shelter, often seen grazing on slopes that are too steep or rocky for crop cultivation. You'll most commonly spot them in Vermont's Green Mountains, New Hampshire's hill country, and the rural areas of western Massachusetts and Connecticut.

seasonality.spring: Lambing season brings new babies to the flock, and recently sheared sheep show off their trim, newly-exposed pink skin. Fresh wool growth begins, appearing as a short, dense fuzz.
seasonality.summer: Sheep seek shade during hot days and their wool grows thick and full. This is peak grazing season when they're most active in early morning and evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Sheep grow their thickest coats in preparation for winter. Many farms bring flocks closer to barns and sheltered areas as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Sheep huddle together for warmth, their thick wool providing excellent insulation. They create distinctive trails through snow as they move between feeding areas and shelter.

funFact: Sheep have rectangular pupils that give them nearly 360-degree vision without moving their heads—they can literally see behind themselves while grazing, making it almost impossible for predators to sneak up on them!
confusionNotes: Sheep are sometimes confused with goats from a distance, but sheep have woolly coats (goats have hair), hold their tails down (goats' tails go up), and have a stockier build. Remember: sheep are 'sheep-ish'—more timid and likely to cluster together, while goats are more independent and adventurous.
contextualKnowledge: While sheep are domesticated animals, occasionally you might encounter feral sheep that have escaped farms and established small wild populations. These animals can survive independently but are still the same species as farm sheep—just living more like their wild ancestors.
compareHints: Domestic sheep are the only members of the Ovis genus you'll encounter in New England, but they're related to wild bighorn sheep found in western North America. Unlike their wild cousins with massive curved horns, most domestic sheep breeds are either hornless or have much smaller, less dramatic horns. Domestic sheep are also much woollier and stockier than their athletic wild relatives.
